speechtext:
And, lest that be misunderstood from the point of view of propriety or otherwise, "royal" is spelled with a small "r".
Sir, a few moments ago I looked up a book on astrology and found the Prime Minister was born under Libra. It is merely coincidence that Libra and liberal have some connection. Those born under Libra, I understand, are clever and have every possibility of manoeuvre. That, too, in connection with the Prime Minister, is merely coincidence.
I hope that his trip to France will be fruitful and beneficial; and if, perchance, to reciprocate General de Gaulle's observation about Canada if he says, "Vive Saskatchewan" or "Vive Prince Albert", I will not object whatsoever. I only hope and expect that the welcome he will receive there will be like the one extended by General de Gaulle to Olive and me, when there on a state visit and with the full realization that that nation was one of the founding nations of our country.
Sir, I extend to the Prime Minister the warmest of good wishes, congratulations, and the hope that during the present parliament success will come by his leadership to this House and our country. Congratulations and the very best!

subsubtopic: ALLEGED MISTREATMENT OF INMATES OF DON JAIL, TORONTO-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to bring a motion in accordance with Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Allegations have been made of invasions of fundamental human rights and police brutality directed against inmates of the Don Jail in the City of Toronto. The matter is, of course, of concern to the provincial authority but it is also of concern to all Canadians since these actions, if the allegations are true, would constitute infringements of the Canadian Bill of Rights passed by this parliament.
There is no room for the emergence in Canada of the grim story of the maltreatment of those in custody of the police which is all too common in other parts of the world. I therefore ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview:
That the Minister of Justice be instructed, in co-operation with the provincial authorities, to ensure that a full and thorough inquiry is made into allegations of brutality directed against inmates of Don Jail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night I stated that I agreed with the general principle of this bill, but found there were serious problems respecting its administration. I wish to speak for a few moments about the necessity of
Federal Business Development Bank Act bringing forward bills like this. The obvious reason is that there has been in the past few years a great change in the capital markets of this country. I think it can be said that in the past money was largely saved and lent in the community in which it was generated. A survey of businesses taken 25 years ago in the community of Dauphin would show they were started with money raised locally. In other words, local capital assisted local business. However, this is no longer the case. We expect the government to step in and provide capital. This is necessary because the practice of registered retirement savings funds, employees pension funds, annuities, mutual funds, and so on, have contributed to the pooling of capital in the large commercial centres of this country. This has been a significant factor in the urbanization of our country.
The time has come to take a second look at the formation and pooling of capital in this country. It is interesting to note that the Investment Dealers Association of Canada recommended to the government the introduction of a plan similar in concept to the registered retirement savings plan and the assisted home ownership plan, both of which are tax deferral savings types of plans. This points up the fact that we are continuing to accept a tax system which is basically a pitch against savings and in favour of spending. Our tax system is a deterrent to saving. A good tax structure should generate enough savings after the payment of taxes to carry on the country's business. The fact that we are involved in this situation shows that our economy is not being run well enough to generate the savings which are necessary for our continued growth.
Much of our inflation can be attributed to government spending. This is made possible by the capacity of the tax system to generate revenue at rates in excess of those projected. The government seems to be caught on a treadmill. They believe that in order to encourage Canadians to save, they must allow them to do it on a pre-tax basis. That is one reason this bill has been brought forward. This measure has been necessitated by the failure of our savings system to provide capital for small businesses. Small business needs much more than this bill in order to be viable. It is caught up in government regulations, labour relations and the fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult to run a small business.

subtopic: FEDERAL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BANK ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to address myself to the bill to incorporate the Federal Business Development Bank. As all hon. members know, the proposed bank is to take over the functions of the present Industrial Development Bank. The Industrial Development Bank has been of benefit to Canadians and others in the establishment of small, medium, and in some cases large businesses in this country when conventional funding has not been available. There are some thoughts I wish to put on record so the minister will have an opportunity to study them before he appears before the committee.
It would be useful to have the allotment of loans in number and amount broken down into more detail than is provided on pages 14 and 15 of the 1973 annual report of the Industrial Development Bank. When this matter goes to committee, the minister and his support staff should indicate the number of applications approved and the number of loans made in each category from zero to


Federal Business Development Bank Act $10,000, $10,000 to $20,000, and each $10,000 range through to $100,000, as well as $100,000 to $250,000.
My concern is that many people believe the Industrial Development Bank lends money to large industries rather than small businesses. The average loan made last year was in the neighbourhood of $48,000. Perhaps it would be appropriate to study this aspect of the bank to ensure that loans are being made to small, individual businesses in Canada.
There has been concern in my constituency, and I understand in other parts of the country, about the amount of red tape involved and the material required by the Industrial Development Bank. I presume the documentation required by this foster child, the Federal Business Development Bank, will also be too onerous for the small business borrower. To prepare the material for a loan of $10,000 to $12,000 requires lawyers and accountants. This eats up a goodly portion of the money borrowed. It is self-defeating to a degree because the whole of the money borrowed does not go into the business; it is eaten up by professional and other studies to determine whether the loan should be made.
It would be appropriate if the regulations under which the proposed bank will carry out its mandate called for less detailed information for small loans and proportionately more for large loans. It would cost less to provide a small amount of information in applying for a small loan, and proportionately more for a greater amount of information required for a large loan.
The Industrial Development Bank is referred to as a bank of last resort; it is a bank for people who have been turned down by conventional lending agencies, trust companies, finance companies, and so on. These are the people who end up at the door of the Industrial Development Bank. This would indicate that applicants were turned down by the conventional lending sources because those institutions were not prepared to take the risk. It therefore appears that the government, by funding the Federal Business Development Bank, is providing money for more venturesome risk enterprises. This is good, and I believe all Canadians appreciate the fact that the government is making these funds available.
In the past, the Industrial Development Bank has been, possibly, too concerned about getting adequate collateral for the loans it has made. It wanted the entire business establishment as collateral, plus an arm and a leg of the principal shareholders, in addition to any other movable or non-movable asset that could be found. In fact, they required more by way of collateral and guarantee than the conventional financial institutions. I hope the officials of the new bank will adopt an easier attitude toward requirements for collateral and personal guarantees, while still using their best business judgment.
There is another matter which concerns me. The federal government is now, of course, involved in lending money to Canadian business to assist the establishment and development of business enterprises in this country. Members in all quarters of the House applaud this decision though in effect it is a housekeeping measure, renaming and redirecting an existing institution.

It should be borne in mind that the conventional lending institutions in Canada, including trust companies and chartered banks, have earned for themselves a strong reputation of helping to finance the sell-out of Canada to foreigners. This has been well documented. I believe most members of this House are aware of instances in which small Canadian firms desiring to expand have had their applications for loans declined by conventional lending institutions. Unfortunately, in these circumstances it frequently happens that United States firms are interested in buying them out or acquiring control. Then if the United States companies turn to the same financial institutions, they find they can get the loans which were denied the original Canadian applicants. This is most unfortunate.
I believe Canadian banks and financial institutions should be playing a more active social role in the development of Canada by and for Canadians. I hope that when the Bank Act comes up for review, a strong, hard look is taken at the way in which the banks in particular are hindering the development of Canada by Canadians. Perhaps there should be forced upon them by the government some restructuring of their philosophy. I am not a person who wants to meddle in business affairs because I believe business can handle itself as a general rule. On the other hand, the government was elected by the people of Canada to provide guidelines within which business should be allowed to operate.
There are one or two statistics I should like to cite in this connection, figures taken from the November, 1970, issue of the Survey of International Business, an official publication of the United States Department of Commerce; they may be somewhat out of date now, but they are nonetheless of interest. They show that in 1963, United States affiliates in Canada generated no less than 83 per cent of their financial requirements in Canada itself, and only 12 per cent in the United States, and that by 1969 the amount of capital generated in Canada had risen to 93 per cent, leaving only 7 per cent to be imported from south of the border. This means, of course, that Canadian institutions are supplying the funds needed by United States affiliates.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me we should do well to consider what Canadians are thinking about foreign ownership in Canada. A poll was taken in the spring of this year by the Gallup organization, the question being: would you favour, or oppose, legislation which would significantly restrict or control further foreign investment in Canada? Nationally, 69 per cent of the Canadian people favoured legislation to control the expansion of foreign ownership. The region in which an affirmative vote was lowest was Quebec, where 54 per cent of those polled were in favour of the legislation. In Atlantic Canada, the figure was 69 per cent; in Ontario, 72 per cent; on the prairies, 71 per cent; and in British Columbia, 77 per cent. This establishes clearly enough that Canadian citizens wish the government and parliament to give directions and guidelines which would increase Canadian control and restrict foreign ownership of the economy.
All parties in this House pay lip service to the merits of Canadian ownership; they favour the idea that Canadian lending institutions should promote Canadian ownership to a far greater extent than at present. Well, we are now


setting up a financial institution to be funded by the government of Canada out of moneys contributed by the taxpayer to the consolidated revenue fund. Yet there is no word in the bill before us which would keep it in line with the intent of Canadians as expressed through polls and by spokesmen from all parties in this House.
I suggest, therefore, that the minister in charge of this bill should himself propose an amendment during the committee stage, one which I believe would prove acceptable to everyone in the committee. What is more, I believe it would be endorsed by the entire Canadian community. What I am suggesting is an amendment to clause 4(1) or to some other clause as might be required. For example, "The objects of the corporation are to promote and assist in the establishment and development of business enterprises in Canada as long as the said business enterprises are owned by Canadian citizens, or landed immigrants within the meaning of the Immigration Act, or a Canadian company, 51 per cent of which is owned by Canadian citizens or landed immigrants". I think that within the scope of the legislation as now drafted, the fact that an application can be made by a foreign company to use the funds of the bank to foster further purchases of Canada by non-residents is regrettable, and I believe an amendment of this nature would be appreciated and accepted by all parties in this House.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to be negative in my approach to foreign investment in Canada. We know we need foreign investment in this country. But it would be much better for Canadians if this investment were financed by money from outside our borders rather than by using our own resources to buy us out.
If an amendment such as I have proposed is put forward and carried in committee or at report stage, it would also have another beneficial aspect; it would make the entire resources of the new Federal Business Development Bank available to Canadians or to landed immigrants who own Canadian companies. In other words, instead of 50 per cent ownership being held by Canadians and 50 per cent by foreign-controlled enterprises or foreign nationals, Canadian ownership would be 100 per cent. It would be money that the government is willing to lend Canadians to help make Canada grow and to build up Canadian ownership of our economy. I, for one, think this would be a very advantageous step.
Some people might say that the government should not involve itself in business decisions. May I point out that the government of this country, as sanctioned by parliament and the people, have already directed themselves in this matter. Today the government are requiring Canadian content in television and radio broadcasting. They have already instigated legislation, now the law of the land, requiring a certain percentage of Canadian ownership in our banks and certain financial institutions. They already require that our uranium companies remain under Canadian control. I think it would be very beneficial to the country and to the bank if this small restriction were imposed. I do not think it would send any shock waves or tidal waves through the business community, but it would guarantee that all the funds of the new Federal Business Development Bank would be available to Canadian citi-
Federal Business Development Bank Act
zens and Canadian-owned companies to enable us to own more of this great land of ours.

subtopic: FEDERAL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BANK ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few brief remarks in connection with the Federal Business Development Bank. In looking over the bill, I note that in clause 4(2) the following is provided:
The corporation in carrying out its objects shall give particular consideration to the needs of small business enterprises.
I think that is an important consideration. There is a need to finance small business in Canada, particularly in western Canada where we do not have, at least in my own province of Saskatchewan, the large type of corporation. I note no interpretation is given of the term "small business enterprise" and I think it would be valuable if such an interpretation were provided in the bill. I also welcome the provisions in the bill pertaining to the managerial advice that might be given to businesses, in the form of counselling and training. This will be welcomed by small businessmen who do not have access to the kind of information and training that is necessary to properly carry on such business.
The basic effect of this bill is to transfer the functions of the Industrial Development Bank from the Bank of Canada to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which I look upon with mixed feelings. Generally speaking, I would think that the Bank of Canada would look upon a business loan in a businesslike way, whereas I am concerned about the kind of bureaucratic build-up that is occurring in many of our government departments today. I hope that by putting the Federal Business Development Bank under the portfolio of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce we will not end up with a bureaucratic nightmare.
I also hope that the board will develop a policy and use the facilities of the bank for the general interest of all Canada, and that it will not be used as a means of furthering the interests of one region of Canada as opposed to another. When the IDB came into being a few years ago, it was initially very popular among the business community in my constituency and was welcomed. But in recent times the IDB has been used less and less. In the province of Saskatchewan, people have been turning to the provincial government organization known as SEDCO-the Saskatchewan Economic Development Corporation.
This situation has concerned me somewhat because SEDCO sometimes requires the transfer or sale to it of certain of the capital stock of the corporation it is lending money to, with the result that the government is getting its fingers into the pie. It is not taking such shares as security for the loan but, rather, is taking them as a condition of making the loan, and the government remains one of the owners of the small business concerned.
I suggest that one of the reasons there has been a movement away from the IDB is that a great deal of documentation is required before a loan is approved. This sometimes takes several months, and businessmen are not always in a position to wait several months for a decision. If a businessman is developing a new business, he is not in a position to wait this length of time, in view of the weather conditions in my part of the country. Not only is


Federal Business Development Bank Act
lengthy documentation required, but as my learned friend who spoke before me mentioned, assets are tied up, including one's arms and legs. The IDB requires stringent personal guarantees and there are many other restrictions. Having talked to accountants in my own constituency, I am convinced this is one reason small businessmen have not been using the IDB.
I believe the lending policies of the Federal Business Development Bank should be economical and that the amount of accounting and legal work should be at a minimum. I believe that the requirement for security should not be restrictive. I hope this will prove to be a bank that businessmen will be able to go to and get a decision as to whether a loan will be approved without undue delay, with the result they will know where they stand.
I have nothing further to add except that I am in support of the bill and will follow with interest the progress of this bank, over the years.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: EXPORT-DEVELOPMENT ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL, CLARIFY DEFINITIONS AND POWERS
speechtext: that Bill C-9, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: EXPORT-DEVELOPMENT ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL, CLARIFY DEFINITIONS AND POWERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the minister is going to speak for the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: EXPORT-DEVELOPMENT ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL, CLARIFY DEFINITIONS AND POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had assumed that there would be unanimity in respect of second reading and reference to the committee, but if hon. members would like some indication of the scope of the bill, I should be pleased to make a few remarks. The purpose of this bill to amend the Export Development Act is to encourage further expansion and diversification of Canada's foreign trade. The impact of these measures will be particularly significant for Canada's capital goods manufacturing and service industries. It is through the development of these industries, to which continuing export markets are so vital, that we can in turn foster the development of Canadian industrial technology and employment opportunities.
Let me also emphasize at this juncture that the size of the financial resources needed is determined not by the control or ownership of the supplier Canadian company or by the financial strength of the foreign borrower-buyer. The size of the financial resources needed is determined by two factors: (a), the vitality and entrepreneurship of Canadian businessmen, big and small, who have identified and are going after export opportunities. Small Canadian businessmen and small Canadian businesses participate as
[Mr. Neil.)
direct beneficiaries in a major way through the operations of the Export Development Corporation. And (b), by the kind of competitive financing provided to their foreign competitors by the government institutions of their foreign competitors.
We are trying to upgrade our raw materials prior to export to assure that the value added in the upgrading process takes place in Canada. We are also striving to increase the export of Canadian manufactured goods for the same reasons. If we are to be successful, the market opportunities for the products of our capital goods industries must be attacked on an internationally competitive basis.
Continued growth and competitiveness of the capital goods and service industries is crucial to the health of the Canadian economy. Hon. members are all aware that Canada has one of the fastest growing labour forces in the industrialized world and one of the largest export sectors, relative to the whole economy, among industrialized countries. The capital goods industries provide many jobs for Canadians either directly or through the demand for components and raw materials. A healthy and growing capital goods industry will be an important element in the continuing implementation of job-creation policies.
In addition to these ongoing needs, should there be a contraction in foreign demand and more intensive international competition in the export markets, a strong export development program will be an essential element in maintaining Canada's international competitiveness and the employment that would be the result.
The Export Development Corporation is a Crown corporation whose purpose is to facilitate and develop export trade by the provision of export-oriented financial facilities. It was established in 1969 as the successor of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. The functions of the corporation are: to make loans to foreign buyers of Canadian capital equipment and services on terms and conditions which are competitive with those offered by other major trading nations in support of their exporters; to insure Canadian firms against non-payment when Canadian goods and services are sold abroad; to guarantee financial institutions against loss when they are involved in financing an export transaction; to insure Canadians against loss of their investments abroad by reason of political actions.
Eighteen months ago, in April, 1973, the House passed amendments to the Export Development Act which provided for an increase in the ceiling on long-term loans and guarantees. At that time the minister of industry, trade and commerce said this was an interim measure and that a more comprehensive bill was being prepared. That comprehensive bill, Bill C-10, was presented to the House during the last parliament but was not considered because of dissolution. Bill C-9 which is presently before the House, with one minor technical change, is the same bill that was given first reading in the last session of parliament as Bill C-10. This technical change was made to avoid potential confusion between the application of the definition of "foreign customer" to the export credits insurance sections of the act versus the long-term financing sections of the act.


The main purpose of the bill, however, remains the same as Bill C-10, and again I commend it to the House. That is, to provide for increases in the corporation's financial ceilings in each of its areas of activity. These increases are required to sustain the expansion of successful Canadian exporter activity and it is intended that these increases serve the requirements of the Canadian exporting community for several years.
In addition, there are a number of technical and administrative amendments proposed, the purpose of which is to clarify some definitions and improve some administrative procedures where experience has shown that a change will enable the Export Development Corporation to serve Canadian exporters and investors more efficiently. I do not propose to deal with these administrative amendments in my remarks today but, rather, will leave them for more detailed elaboration in committee.
The export credits insurance facility applies mainly to exports of commodities, manufactured goods and services which are sold on short and medium credit terms; that is, up to five years. The present ceilings total $1 billion. This is made up of $500 million for the corporation's risk- sections 24 to 26-and $500 million for the government's risk-sections 27 and 28-the latter being for situations that are not normally appropriate for the corporation's account but which, in the opinion of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the cabinet, are in the national interest. It is proposed that the ceiling for each of these sections be raised from $500 million to $750 million, increasing the total export credit insurance facility from $1 billion to $1.5 billion.
When speaking of expanded EDC activity, attention is usually focused on the growth of its long-term lending. I shall be speaking of this shortly. But it is also important to realize that there has been important growth in the sector of exports covered by the insurance program. In 1973, the volume of exports insured was $565 million, more than double the amount of five years ago, and prospects are that the volume of coverage for 1974 will exceed $700 million. Consequently, there is need to increase the insurance ceilings to provide adequately for continued growth in the years ahead.
The facility for long-term loans and guarantees applies to exports of capital goods and services which customarily justify credit terms in excess of five years. The current ceilings total $1,950 million, made up of $1,500 million for section 29-corporate account-and $450 million for section 31-government account. It is proposed that these ceilings be raised from $1,500 million to $4,250 million for section 29, and from $450 million to $850 million for section 31, increasing the total lending ceiling from $1,950 million to $5.1 billion.
This increase may be startling to hon. members, and indeed it is one of major significance. The dimension of the increase is a function of two factors: a change in the definition of the ceiling and, more importantly, a reflection of the remarkable success of Canadian capital equipment and service suppliers in winning contracts abroad.
Hon. members may recall that last year there was considerable difficulty in comprehending exactly where the
Federal Business Development Bank Act corporation stood in relation to its ceiling for long-term lending. This was because the ceiling as currently defined relates to notes outstanding and not, as we now propose, to signed loan agreements. The difficulty arises because notes become outstanding as the corporation makes disbursements, and this often extends for a very considerable period of time after the signing of a loan agreement; in some cases as long as five or six years. During that period the corporation is also receiving repayments on signed agreements, which reduces the gross amount of notes outstanding. Consequently, the net amount of notes outstanding that will ultimately result from a given level of signed financing agreements is, practically speaking, always less than the total amount of those signed agreements. Therefore, we are proposing to redefine the ceiling in terms of signed agreements net of repayments-a number which can instantly be ascertained and related without confusion to the ceiling.
The most important reason for increased ceilings, however, is the remarkable continuing success of our capital goods and services producers in winning overseas orders. These exporters include suppliers of engineering and technical services; transportation equipment such as ships, aircraft, locomotives and off-highway vehicles; telecommunications equipment; heavy duty electrical goods and power generation equipment, including our CANDU nuclear power system; foreign industries equipment; steel mills, and a variety of other items related to such areas as chemical pollution control and scientific research.
Our manufacturers have penetrated new foreign markets and developed a momentum of success which has resulted in the employment of a significant number of skilled Canadians. An essential element of this success has been the availability of internationally competitive longterm financing from EDC. During the 1960s, long-term financing averaged approximately $50 million a year, but in 1970 it reached $100 million. It has grown markedly in each subsequent year, and in 1973 signed loan agreements totalled $463 million.
Prospects for 1974 are that EDC's long-term lending will exceed $1 billion. This is expected to be made up of approximately $650 million under section 29, and some $400 million under section 31. This is an unprecedented level of capital goods export activity, but all current indications are that these levels can be sustained and in fact may grow in future years. Therefore, the levels of the new ceilings being proposed are necessary to accommodate this activity, and it is expected that they will provide a reasonable period of some three to five years before the ceilings may again have to be reviewed by parliament.
The need for the new ceilings is more urgent than might appear on the surface. The $1 billion of 1974 lending relates to projects which have been before EDC for a long period of time. In addition to this, there is more than another $1 billion in the pipeline at various stages of development. New projects continue to come forward every day. The point is that there is a long gestation period between an initial inquiry seeking confirmation of financing availability and the signing of an agreement. EDC is virtually committed against its present ceilings and difficulties could arise if new legislation is not forthcoming at this time. It is important to ensure that we do


Federal Business Development Bank Act not risk disruption in the continuity of our capital goods export sales.
The foreign investment insurance program was established in 1969 and is the newest of EDC's facilities. The current ceiling is $150 million and it is proposed that this be increased to $250 million. At present, there are some $30 million of policies outstanding, with a further $125 million of projects under active consideration. The amount of the proposed increase in the ceiling is intended to provide for future requirements over at least a three-year period, and will facilitate the entry of Canadian firms into international joint ventures.
Such joint ventures are suited to Canadian commercial policy and the development policies of most foreign governments because local knowledge and capital supplied by resident partners can be blended with Canadian capital and engineering technology. In fact, in most countries today a joint venture is the only viable vehicle for facilitating Canadian investments in foreign markets. The joint venture ensures a foreign country of a real commitment on the part of Canadian engineers and management and protects the Canadian equity position.
An expanded foreign investment insurance service as provided by Bill C-9 will help to encourage and facilitate sound Canadian joint ventures in other countries. It is a fact of life that official support is provided by all major countries in support of their exports. These arrangements exist to make financial services available to cover risk and provide credit terms which are more favourable than the facilities normally available in the private sector. The existence of such official support means that Canadian exporters need the same package of financial services in order to compete effectively.
These services are needed because the foreign buyer considers both the commercial contract and the financial terms offered and then compares this over-all package to that offered by, for instance, the Japanese, the Americans or the French, all of whom provide substantial support for their exporters. Hon. members should be aware that lack of fully competitive export financing facilities in Canada would critically impair the ability of Canadian capital goods and services industry to compete internationally.

subtopic: EXPORT-DEVELOPMENT ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL, CLARIFY DEFINITIONS AND POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose for lunch I was just making the point that hon. members should be aware that lack of a fully competitive export financing facility in Canada would critically impair the ability of the Canadian capital goods and services industry to compete internationally.
It should be emphasized that the services of EDC are not provided to buy foreign orders with cheap financing; that is, EDC only matches foreign competition, it does not

undercut it. EDC financing is only available for exporters who are thoroughly competitive on the commercial fundamentals of price, quality, delivery and after-sales services. With the continuing need in Canada to provide skilled employment, a healthy capital goods order book will be a valuable hedge against the possibility of contractions on foreign demand. In such a situation, the international competition for export orders will be intense. A strong EDC program will be an essential element in maintaining Canada's international competitiveness.
In the discharge of this very important function, EDC will work increasingly closely with the Canadian chartered banks and it is EDC policy to seek maximum private sector participation in a loan, consistent with providing internationally competitive financing.
[DOT] (MIO)
The combination of private sector and EDC financing is structured in each case to match the financing offered by the official support institution of other competing countries. EDC lending is basically undertaken on the authority of its board of directors. The board of directors is composed of senior government officials as well as representatives of the Canadian private sector. EDC operates according to commercial criteria. It does not make imprudent loans to secure capital goods business at any cost. EDC requires that the terms of the loan be appropriate to the transaction and consistent with international practice, and that the project for which the loan is made is commercially viable. EDC is prudent in arranging for the security of its commitments and frequently obtains unconditional government or central bank guarantees of payment.
Hon. members are aware that the government's proposal for a Federal Business Development Bank-which was dealt with just before the present bill was introduced

is to assist small businesses in their domestic endeavours. We also have the program for export market development and, in addition, a complete range of EDC services to assist small businesses in their export activities. There is a very considerable degree of small business involvement with the export credits insurance program. At the end of 1973, 939 insurance policies were outstanding. Of this number, 727 were short-term relating mainly to sales of consumer goods, and 212 were issued for capital goods and services. Fifty-six per cent of the consumer goods policies were issued for an annual export sales volume of under $100,000, while 33 per cent of the capital goods policies were for sales of goods and services each under $100,000.
In addition to these insurance facilities, EDC also makes long-term loans or guarantees directly to foreign borrowers to finance exports of capital goods and services sold by small Canadian business. For instance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), announced earlier this year in Winnipeg that EDC made a loan of $500,000 to Poland for the purchase of pre-stressed concrete manufacturing equipment from Spiroll Corporation of Winnipeg.
As a further indication of EDC's ability and willingness to assist small business, the corporation-and this is a very recent decision of the board-will provide financing for capital projects irrespective of size, including those below $1 million, provided of course that the project war-


rants long-term financing on the basis of internationally accepted criteria. In the past, some hon. members have focused on this particular facility and alleged that, in dollar volume, few loans seem to have been made in support of sales by small businesses. When the situation is properly analysed, one realizes that long-term financing- that is, on terms in the range of 5 to 15 years-is generally appropriate, whether speaking domestically or internationally, for larger transactions.
I have pointed out that in the short and medium term credit areas, EDC is heavily involved with small business through its insurance program. This is not to say, however, that small business does not benefit importantly from the long-term financing facility. The exporter of record may often be a large firm located in a major industrial area, but the chain of sub-suppliers extends to all parts of Canada and down to the smallest of Canadian manufacturers. This effect is reinforced by EDC's minimum 80 per cent Canadian content policy. For instance, a CANDU nuclear power system sale would involve upward of 200 Canadian suppliers, with contracts ranging as low as $500.
Our success in sustaining high employment and meaningful growth over the longer term will depend on our success in stimulating the growth of the right kind of industries. For the 1980s and beyond, these are industries that do more than just create jobs. They must create jobs for an increasingly well trained labour force which, in turn, is essential in order to keep Canada in the forefront of high-technology industries. But it is these industries that more often than not depend on continuous access to foreign markets in order to stay competitive. Just one example is our engineering consultants. An increasing number of them are working all over the world, and indeed so they must if they are to stay pre-eminent in their fields. It is, of course, precisely in this sector of high-technology capital goods and services industries that EDC support is essential. If this support were withdrawn or curtailed in the interests of short-term considerations, the damage to our long-term development prospects would be out of all proprotion to whatever short-term benefits might be realized or thought to be realized.
To put it another way, either export markets are essential to the long-term well-being of a particular company, or not. Where they are essential, the company must maintain and try to expand its foothold in foreign markets on a continuing basis. International business is much too competitive to allow us the luxury to venture abroad when it is convenient, for instance when economic activity is slack at home, and to stay out of foreign markets when domestic demand is brisk.
Also, in considering an expanded rate of activity for the EDC at a time when inflationary pressures are still strong in Canada as elsewhere, it is important to differentiate between what economists are fond of calling macro-economic and micro-economic considerations. Anti-inflationary fiscal and monetary measures, to be effective, must affect the aggregate of economic activity. But it would be a serious mistake to attempt to further strengthen these measures by depriving individual companies of EDC support and, hence, of their ability to compete abroad. It is for this reason that I am proposing increases in EDC insurance, lending and guarantee ceilings that are quite sub-
Federal Business Development Bank Act stantial. The Canadian firms who utilize EDC's services continue to be required to meet stringent criteria relating to the benefit of an EDC-supported transaction to Canada and Canadian industrial development objectives.
Once an applicant meets these criteria, it would not make sense economically, nor would it be fair to individual exporters, if ceiling were set too low relative to expected demand. Of equal importance, the annual allocation of funds to EDC must of necessity reflect not only the trade opportunities available to our firms, and our long-term development objectives, but also the realities of domestic monetary and fiscal policies. Hon. members should appreciate that what is sought is a balance between the situation of the moment and the requirements of Canada's future.
In conclusion, let me emphasize that the Export Development Corporation has an essential role to play in the industrial development of Canada. The next few years are critical in this development, but they hold considerable opportunity to develop export markets as our own manufacturing industries build on the base of our resources. The provisions of this bill will ensure that the facilities of EDC are available to capitalize to the fullest extent the opportunities of the coming years.
Hon. members will recall that last year the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said that a general review of the corporation's activity would be possible when this bill was brought forward. The House may consider that this should be done in the standing committee. The minister has indicated to me that he looks forward to that opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of assisting exports by making loans to foreign customers who buy Canadian goods and services has long been supported by members in all parts of this House. In putting this principle into practice, the emphasis should be on helping small and medium-sized Canadian producers make export sales abroad because of their greater need for this kind of assistance. I think all hon. members agree that the big producers are far better able to arrange, through regular commercial channels, the financing necessary to make sales in the export field. Therefore, the chief objection which the official opposition finds in the legislation before the House is that it


Federal Business Development Bank Act
contains no provisions to make export financing available for orders of less value than $1 million.
I checked this recently with an official of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He has charge of these matters. He told me that this is not in the bill, but it is a corporate procedure followed by the Export Development Corporation and that in fact the Export Development Corporation does not provide export financing for orders below $1 million. This makes it impossible for small businesses to participate to the extent they should in obtaining export orders.
In the United States, the Export-Import Bank places no lower limit on the dollar value of a sale which it will assist. It carries out this kind of assistance by means of its Co-operative Financing Facility, which the Export-Import Bank outlines as follows. I quote from their operational directive:
With its Co-operative Financing Facility (CFF) the Export-Import Bank of the United States helps make credit available to small and medium-size purchasers of U.S. equipment and related services through banks in their own countries.
The CFF concept is simple: Eximbank arranges the co-operation of financial institutions (CIs) abroad to extend loans at their own risk to purchasers of U.S. exports. Eximbank in turn lends these CIs half the funds at a low rate of interest-currently 6 per cent per annum. The CIs provide the other half from their own resources.
If a Cl wishes to borrow its half of the financing, Eximbank can assist by guaranteeing repayment to another lender of these funds.
The CFF accomplishes the following:
It brings Eximbank financing to the doorsteps of small and medium-size enterprises that might not otherwise be able to purchase U.S. goods and services. All a buyer need do is call on a Cl in his own area. The Cl's familiarity with the customer's credit standing and local market conditions enables it to reach a decision quickly on the loan request.
The CFF enables a Cl to-
1.	Broaden its lending capacity;
2.	Increase its resources;
3.	Develop new relations with existing customers; and
4.	Attract new ones.
It helps U.S. suppliers expand their exports and services to enterprises which lack experience in financing overseas purchases. Many enterprises find working with their own bank the most convenient way to obtain their financing.
The next part is very important.
There is no upper or lower limit to the size of an export loan within the agreed total.
A cash payment by the Cl's customer of 10 per cent is required for each transaction. Thus, Eximbank's portion of an export loan will equal 45 per cent of the export sale.
Thus, we see that by making use of the commercial banks in the countries concerned, the Export-Import Bank achieved two very important objectives. The first is that by having the local commercial bank cover half the loan, the capital which is made available by the government for assisting the export program can be spread over twice the volume of contracts which would otherwise be possible. The second benefit is that there is no need for a lower limit to the size of orders that can be handled, because the local bank investigates the credit worthiness of the proposed transaction and, because of its local knowledge of the applicant and the project for which the financing is requested, there is no problem in handling relatively small orders.
The program I have described has worked very satisfactorily in the United States for many years, and losses have been minimal. There is no reason why such a program will not work equally well in this country. It would provide a much needed service, which would greatly increase the ability of small and medium-sized Canadian producers to obtain export orders which are essential if production and employment are to keep up to a satisfactory level in this country. The benefits of such a program are obvious: it would bring increased employment, taxes and profits because of the additional business for this country.
In order to greatly assist small and medium-sized businesses to obtain export orders by the use of export financing, I intend when the bill reaches committee to move an amendment. This amendment will incorporate into the bill the original intention of parliament that there should be no discrimination against small and medium-sized businesses in the form of a floor below which credit terms are not available for potential export orders.

Again, I recognize that in the competitive system of trade which exists in the world today, Canada cannot be the one country which abstains from a form of subsidy, but I believe an attempt should be made to diminish its level under international agreement, even if it cannot be removed entirely. How-
Federal Business Development Bank Act ever, the main emphasis of what I have to say concerns a different subject. I want to talk about the political implications of the bill before us in the international world, rather than about its strictly economic effects.
Some two years ago the government put out a paper on foreign policy, listing a number of goals. One of these goals was economic growth, another was social justice and a third, I think, was peace and security. The provisions of this bill and, indeed, the objects of the department which produced it-the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-seem to be exclusively concerned with economic growth. We do not, of course, deny the importance of economic growth, but we do insist there are some issues of social justice which should take priority over economic growth, in the basic interests of our country as well as of the world as a whole.
In a speech he made in June to the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, in effect, that the basis of Canadian foreign policy would be considerations of a humanistic and compassionate nature. The right hon. gentleman spoke with extreme eloquence, and no doubt I have not captured his exact words. But what do we find in this bill? We find that loans are extended to countries without any consideration being given to the political consequences of so doing. If the minister were here, I imagine he would say that these considerations of a political nature are rigidly excluded from any judgment as to who should and who should not be given a loan. We think that this is wrong, and I should like to give an illustration.
A little more than one year ago, on September 11, 1973, a military coup took place in Chile. We believe that Canadian policy under this act may be used to bolster the regime which came into power at that time. Social justice was forgotten. Since the coup, a consistent pattern of violation of human rights and the total suppression of democratic institutions has developed in Chile.

speechtext:
Exactly. Many of us have received personal and well documented accounts of the present reign of terror-arbitrary arrests, detention without trial, systematic torture, and summary executions. I could cite authorities, but I think they are well known-for example, Amnesty International and the International Commission of Jurists have made reports fully substantiating what I have said.
The Canadian government almost immediately-and perhaps it was within its rights to do so-recognized the military junta. The then minister said that recognition does not imply approval. But economic aid does imply approval. I believe that economic aid to the military junta in Chile in the form of grants,- loans, credits and investments strengthens the position of an oppressive regime in that country.
The military junta has embarked upon a program of free enterpriserTt seeks foreign investment. While it does, the cost of life's basic necessities rises uncontrollably. Wages and most incomes are controlled and depressed. Unemployment has multiplied as the result of mass firings and


Federal Business Development Bank Act
student expulsions. Trade unions and other means of representing the rights and needs of working people have been repressed and made illegal. So foreign aid enables this junta to continue its repressive policy.
Which international institutions are doing this? One of them is the Export Development Corporation which we are discussing today. As long ago as September, 1973, the same month as the coup, an export credit of $5 million was arranged for the purchase of de Havilland aeroplanes. This was not cancelled, though no deliveries had been made at the time of the coup. We would like an assurance from the minister at some stage that the Export Development Corporation is not going to continue a policy of financing repression and suppression of fundamental human rights by this sort of aid.
Then there is the question of private enterprise. I believe that part of this act is used to insure against loss of investments abroad through political risks. I do not know what is meant by "political risks", but it is a pretty broad definition, so evidently some political judgment is involved in granting this insurance. For example, it was recently announced that Falconbridge Nickel Mines were considering a $300 million investment in copper production in Chile. Well, I suppose that is their business. If that is what they want to do, then they should do it. But I do not think they need one dollar of support from the public treasury in making that investment in Chile, and I hope they are not getting it under the guise of some foreign insurance or foreign loan made available under concessions granted by this act.
The main point I am trying to make is that this act should not operate in isolation from other policies of the government. If the policy of the government, as the Prime Minister says, is based primarily on social justice, then considerations of social justice must come into the external operations of the Canadian government.
There must be adequate co-ordination between the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-a department which, by its very name, considers merely economic matters-and the Department of External Affairs, CIDA and other appropriate agencies, to ensure they are working together to build a better world, rather than using this agency to protect and sustain regimes that we abhor and which have been denounced by international tribunals.
These are the sort of doubts, difficulties and hesitations that we have about this type of legislation. It is not new legislation. The bill before us is amending legislation that increases the capital available. We do not think now is the time to seek to strike at the principle of the act, but we do urge the government to look into the questions I have raised and to give assurances to the House so that we can support what should be a program of assistance to small and medium-sized businesses in Canada to expand their exports. This principle is admirable and it has our support. But we do not want to find ourselves giving subsidies to people who do not need them, for purposes that we do not approve.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In answer to my question as to what in fact is the ceiling under section 29 of the existing Export Development Act and whether that ceiling has been exceeded, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury), acting for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, indicated that the notes outstanding at the present time amount to $710 million as of September 30, I believe he said. I point out that at the end of December, 1973, the notes amounted to $541 million, so we can see there has been an increase of approximately $160 million in notes.
I think it is significant that we have had demonstrated to us today how little ministers of the Crown really understand the operations of the Export Development Corporation. The fact is that Mr. Granby stated in Vancouver yesterday that they are lending over $1 billion this year alone. If you were to add this $1 billion in 1974 to the amount of loans outstanding at the end of December, 1973, it shows total liabilities and loans are over $1.5 billion. The current ceiling is $1.5 billion. In short, once again the government has violated the law of the land in its anxiety to dish out funds around the world through this corporation.
I think it is particularly pertinent to note that if the definition referred to by the Minister of Public Works is interpreted the way he desires then parliament was misled when the government last introduced this bill. At that time the ceiling under Section 29 was $850 million. We were told that if we did not pass the amendment loans would exceed that ceiling within a few months. Yet today we are told that loans as of September 30 still amount to only $710 million. In short, if he is right in his present interpretation, there was no need for the amendment to


the act in the early part of 1973 because loans are still below the old ceiling.
My colleague has already mentioned two very important changes we would like to see in this bill. When considering this legislation we should also consider what has taken place in respect to the administration of the Export Development Corporation. It is nice to sit and listen to the syrup handed out by the minister about how beautiful it is to have this type of lending facility. I noticed that he did not tell us about the champagne parties that take place at the EDC offices every time one of these agreements is signed, but we should point out to the Canadian public the kind of loans the corporation has been extending.
Would the average Canadian be willing to lend his pro rate share of $82.4 million to Iran? I would be very interested in knowing the reaction of the average Canadian to that question. Last spring $82.5 million in Canadian funds was loaned to Iran so that country could rebuild or build a forestry industry. The cost of this money to Canada through the EDC was something in the neighbourhood of 9 per cent to 10 per cent. As we all know, even Canada Savings Bonds are yielding 9% per cent. If you add an administrative charge of 1 per cent that means a total cost to the Canadian treasury of 103A per cent for the money the government of Canada has to borrow. The average cost of loans to Iran was 7 per cent. One can see from that alone that the Canadian public has been subsidizing Iran to the extent of 33/4 per cent on the $82.5 million loan.
For what purpose does Iran need money when, in the current year, it has enjoyed a budgetary surplus of $8 billion? If anybody should be lending funds, Iran should be lending them to Canada.
In this regard let us look at an article appearing in the current issue of Newsweek. We must keep in mind that not only $82.5 million was loaned to Iran but there have been several other loans made to Iran, for example a couple amounting to $2.1 million at 63A per cent interest, the benefactor in Canada being General Motors Corporation, the largest multinational corporation in the world.
While this government has chosen Iran as the recipient of almost $100 million in loans. The article in Newsweek points out that:
-the Shah .. . spearheaded the oil-producing nations' move to quadruple prices and . .. has since argued that the already stratospheric cost of oil should go even higher.
The article goes on to point out:
-even as the Shah was lecturing the superpowers, his emissaries continued to use their wealth to buy influence in the west-pledging $75 million to America's foundering Grumman Corp. The strategy fitted neatly into the pattern that the Shah has drawn for himself since the oil-producing nations imposed their embargo. Iran already has the largest military force in the Persian Gulf, but the Shah has set out on a damn-the-cost buying spree to increase his military arsenal. Last year alone, Iran spent $4 billion for U.S. weaponry, making the Shah the No. 1 foreign buyer of American military equipment.
Just imagine, we are lending money, nearly $100 million, to a country which in turn can afford to buy $4 billion worth of military equipment from the United States in one year. That is almost double the total national defence budget of this country for one year.
That money was used to buy 80 Grumman F-14s, 209 Phantom jets, 500 attack helicopters, 700 tanks and six
Federal Business Development Bank Act destroyers. One official was quoted in this Newsweek article as having said:
"The Shah's power is growing enormously ... We may be creating a Frankenstein monster."
The article goes on to state:
In addition to his store of U.S.-supplied arms, the Shah has built up the world's largest Hovercraft fleet, capable of landing a battalion of troops on the Arab side of the gulf within 25 minutes.
The article then states:
The Shah is also using his immense oil wealth ($20 billion a year) in other ways as he seeks to expand his sphere of influence. Iran has pumped $3 billion into Italy for joint business ventures, $1.2 billion into Britain in industrial loans, $1 billion into France in partial advance payment for five nuclear reactors and more than $7 billion into developing nations . .. The Iranians have also given $1 billion to the the World Bank, $1 million to George Washington University to train Iranian students-
Later the article goes on to state:
The Shah has also turned to private companies in seeking an outlet for his cash surplus. Less than three months ago, Iran purchased a 25 per cent interest in West Germany's giant Krupp Steel Works for more than $100 million.
Perhaps that is how our money was used, to pick up that 25 per cent interest for Iran in the Krupp Steel Works. The article then states:
Such massive investment at a time when Iranian oil prices are helping to undermine the Western economy may seem contradictory. But, in fact, it is in keeping with the Shah's tendency to play both sides against the middle.
I suggest that no other government has been an easier mark than the Canadian government in respect of this type of soft-lending activity.
The article goes on to speak of the opulence of the Shah, stating:
"At one party in a sizeable palace, everything that was not actually gold seemed to be marble or something equally precious. And the tiered rose garden leading to the olympic-size swimming pool was straight out of a 'Great Gatsby' set-as were the expensive-looking guests."
I point that out because it is typical of the present Liberal government. It adopts something which is good in concept, and certainly it is good to support Canadian exporters, particularly our small ones, but that does not mean that millions of dollars should be loaned to countries, such as Iran, which are obviously not in dire straits. Let us think of the consequences of a billion dollars being loaned this year alone.
A billion dollars this year, as was pointed out by Mr. Granby, compares with $50 million, a year in the 1960's. In today's inflationary times, on the average loan that the Export Development Corporation is making we find that the real dollars that will be returned to Canadians, after you put in an appropriate deflator for 1973-and I only use 1973, not 1974-result in a $576 million lost on $1 billion worth of lending activities by the time these loans are repaid in real buying power.
Second, I have already indicated that when we borrow at 93A per cent, charge a 1 per cent administration charge, and then lend the funds at 7 per cent, we are losing almost at the rate of 4 per cent a year on the loan itself. When that calculation is added to the one that I have just done


Federal Business Development Bank Act to give us real buying power with respect to $1 billion worth of loans, we find that the Canadian public will have either subsidized or lost its buying power to the extent of $918 million in respect of the $1 billion that is being put out by the corporation this year.
Surely it is madness for a government to act so irresponsibly, bearing in mind that my figures are based on the assumption that all the loans will be repaid. The fact is that the Export Development Corporation already has loans in default on its books. It already has loans which have required renegotiation in order to put them into an apparent current status. I would suggest that this is a Crown corporation that deserves extensive study, review, and better management than we have been seeing over the past few years.
I have referred to the fact that we borrow these funds to put into the Export Development Corporation, but here again I think the extent to which the government has been borrowing funds in Canada is often not realized. Before it took power the total liabilities of the present federal government were in the $30 billion category. In 1973 those liabilities amounted to $51,695 million. These were the gross borrowings of the Trudeau Liberal government. I understand that by the end of this year they will be nearly $55 billion in size. In short, in a peacetime period the government has incurred liabilities on behalf of the Canadian public to the tune of approximately $25 billion.
Now we have legislation before us in the form of this bill in which it is contemplating one Crown corporation alone having the capability to lend up to $5 billion of Canadian taxpayer's funds. Surely my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), are justified in saying that this legislation deserves close scrutiny when it goes to committee. I say "when it goes to committee" because obviously, with the brutal majority that the government has in this parliament, there is nothing that members on this side of the House can do effectively to restrain the arrogant, incompetent management shown by the government today.

speechtext: But it is you who called the election.

subtopic: EXPORT-DEVELOPMENT ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL, CLARIFY DEFINITIONS AND POWERS
speechtext:
When we refer to this type of funding, let us think of what $1 billion, and certainly $5 billion could do if it were spent within Canada. Every time one of our large urban municipal centres comes to Ottawa and asks: have you funds to help our urban transportation or help with our sewage and water capital expenditures, the answer is a flat no. Think what would be the effect if part of the money that is being earmarked for those multinational corporations could be earmarked for some Canadian activity, for example helping municipalities develop urban transportation systems, or sewage and water systems.
There is an energy crisis in the country. Would it not make better sense if this type of funding were made available here instead of being lent to the tune of almost $100 million to oil rich Iran? Would it not be better if we tried to use some funding to help in the production of atomic plants in this country, or in the development of new energy sources? We must bear in mind that not only are these kinds of funds being denied to urban centres but we find that there is a great deal of discrimination.

Just before this bill came up for second reading we dealt with the bill that is transforming, in some ways, the Industrial Development Bank. What a contrast there is between the government's attitude when its friends in the big business community need help and assistance, and its attitude when the small businessmen of Canada need some help and assistance.
I have indicated that the average interest on loans so far of the Export Development Corporation is around 7 per cent per annum, and yet the average loan of the Industrial Development Bank is at 11 per cent at present. We find that the loans through the Export Development Corporation in the last year which I have reviewed benefitted only 43 customers in Canada, but the loans through the IDB benefitted 16,075. What a distinction! The average loan made by the Export Development Corporation-including the one to Iran-is $23.3 million, but the average loan made through IDB is $45,000. That is the Trudeau government in action. You can certainly see where its sympathies lie.
I notice that in introducing this bill the Minister of Public Works said that all they are doing is simply following the competitive practices of various other nations in the world and that we have to keep up our end. What nonsense! Let me point out that in today's Globe and Mail, if the minister has not already noticed, it is said that the World Bank is lending its funds at 8 per cent. So why are we still lending funds at 7 per cent? Who is leading to whom? Perhaps certain of the investor nations in the world are correct in saying that Canada has done more to help soften financing than any other industrial nation in the world. That is a far cry from the suggestion that we are simply following. I suggest that we are doing an awful lot of leading. We are into reckless, irresponsible lending activities in this type of financing.
I mention this because, as I have indicated, with the brutal majority that the Trudeau Liberals have in parliament they can put through this type of legislation. They can run the Export Development Corporation as they see fit, and I suggest that over the past few years it has been poorly run.
But I want it placed on the record that while we are forced to pass this legislation, because we have no alternative, there will be a day of reckoning and this House, or certainly a subsequent parliament, will have to explain to the Canadian public why there have been write offs of tens of millions of dollars in loans that are being made at the current time to countries that will never repay the debt. In any event, the fact is that with buying power falling as it is, in an inflationary period such as the one in which we are living now, we cannot win if the Export Development Corporation continues to act as irresponsibly as it has done in the past few years.
I hope some skill will go into the operation of this corporation. I hope too that the government will at least give us a better opportunity than it gave us last time at committee stage to hear witnesses, to question certain of the officials of the Export Development Corporation and


to get a few of the facts-even the ugly facts-out on the table concerning this operation.

the Export Development Act to increase the authorized share capital of the Corporation from $125,000,000 to $400,000,000 and to permit the Minister designate to subscribe for shares with payments out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund;-
-or the taxpayers' credit-

Mr. Speaker, as I said a while ago, I listened with great interest to the minister's speech. He stated that we do lack export facilities, which has lost us several foreign markets because, as the minister said, we lack organization and export facilities.
He said that Canadian companies must have access to the export services to be able to compete with other countries. He even mentioned the employment opportunities that the adoption of this bill would bring to the country.
The minister even established a parallel with Bill C-14 to incorporate the Federal Business Development Bank by saying that this bill would help Canada's small and medium-sized businesses. But if we are content to listen to the minister and do not read each line of the bill, we shall say: What the minister has just said is great. This bill will protect the small businesses through the Federal Development Bank. After reading Bill C-9 and listening to the explanations given by the minister, I thought that small businesses would finally have the protection that they have needed for many years.
Mr. Speaker, this bill includes no provisions for orders lower than $1 million. This is why, after hearing the spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative and New Democratic Parties, I wish to associate myself with them and ask the minister to bring an amendment to this bill, because it is impossible to do so in committee, which amendment would make the provisions of the bill available to the small Canadian industries. Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for small industries to benefit from this act if its provisions are restricted to $1 million orders.
The small industries who have sales of $400,000 or $600,000 will not be able to benefit from this act. In my opinion, this is very important and I therefore wish to comment specifically on this subject and to defend the small industry, because since my arrival in this House, I have heard
Canada Pension Plan
people say: The small industry will finally be protected. When it comes to acting, Mr. Speaker, it is always zero. It is always the same old thing.
The hon. member who spoke before me said to the minister that in the past the Export Act had greatly favoured the multinational corporations. And how! If it is true that we loaned $17 million to 43 companies, there cannot be many small businesses that got the benefit of these loans.
That is why it is urgent to call on the minister today so that he can go before the committee to reduce this amount in favour of small businesses so that, as the minister himself said, they may also sell on the export market and benefit from these loans guaranteed by the taxpayers's money.
If we do not manage to amend this law in this way, it will be detrimental to our Canadian businesses. It is useless to work and discuss and especially present laws that we say are made to favour small business when it is quite the opposite that happens. All I want and all I hope is that the minister will introduce these amendments himself before the committee and that he will make this law more accessible to small businesses so that they might at last reach the adult stage and not always die as teenagers.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister will make a note of these remarks. I am only hoping for one thing, but I hope the minister will grant our requests.
