subtopic: ENVIRONMENT

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider setting up, in co-operation with the provinces, an Institute of Human Environmental Studies to determine, among other matters (a) the degree of air, soil, water and noise pollution the human species can tolerate without serious effects on physical and mental health (b) the type of environment which stimulates the most desirable qualities of physical and mental health in the human species (c) the type of national development which would give satisfactory environment to the greatest possible number of Canadians (d) the minimum of modifications to the present day indiscriminate and largely unplanned growth of our metropolitan areas necessary to put within reach of the inhabitants of these areas a quality of environment which would provide (i) adequate housing (ii) adequate recreational facilities, including parkland (iii) adequate social infra-structure, such as transportation, education, hospital and recreation facilities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have no illusions that what I am about to say will cause a sensation, or even that it will arouse interest, especially at this stage on Friday afternoon. However, I feel a strong urge to put forth my views on what I consider a question of vast importance to Canada even if nobody notices what I have to say, and even if mine turns out to be a lone voice crying in the wilderness.
I consider that, in the long run, the greatest tragedy that has happened to our country since World War II has been that most of our national growth has taken place in a few large centres, instead of being more evenly spread throughout the length and breadth of this great country. The tragedy has been deepened by the fact that most of this growth has been haphazard and irrational-growth for growth's sake-with no clearly defined objectives of benefit for this or future generations.
Almost three-quarters of our population now live in cities and towns. This is not necessarily bad, but it is forecast that by 1980 nearly two-thirds of all Canadians will live in 29 major urban communities, and one-third will live in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
I am a countryman living in the countryside, representing a rural riding, and you may wonder, Mr. Speaker, why I should be concerned. I am concerned for two major reasons. I do not believe that the megalopolis is the environment in which the average person who makes up the mass of people has a reasonable prospect of attaining an acceptable quality of life. Nor is it an environment in which the average person can attain that measure of self-fulfilment and sense of purpose that is necessary for contentment and peace of mind. I think the present generation senses this.
I noticed a phenomenon in my constituency in Prince Edward Island where log cabins are being built on odd pieces of land here and there. Young people are going back to nature and living in the most primitive ways. These are not local people from nearby farms or communities. In almost every case they have come from Montreal, Toronto,



New York or Los Angeles. As a result of this phenomenon, my closest neighbour has come from Los Angeles.
It is at least arguable that it is a pity so many Canadians and future generations are condemned by fickle chance to be forced to live in the kind of environment created by the megalopolis.
As far as national growth is concerned, we as a nation have taken the course of least resistence. We have let our country, like Topsy, just grow. I am not against growth. I believe that the very essence of life at any level is planned, programmed, meaningful growth toward a known objective for a beneficial purpose. However, I do not believe in wild, malignant, open-ended growth like that of a cancerous cell-growth for growth's sake.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Humanity has been on this planet for a long time. If we represent that span of time by one day, 24 hours, we will find that the first cities come into being at about five minutes to midnight. Therefore, in the whole development of humanity, cities have had a very short experience.
In the past cities have been the nurseries of civilization as we know it. However, most of the advantages of the early city-security, ease of communications and ease of transportation-are no longer valid. I think that perhaps modern technology has made the megalopolis as obsolete as the medieval castle was made by the development of the cannon.
We should also note that the record of all past civilizations has been that they collapsed when they became highly urbanized. We should try to determine if there is a cause and effect relationship here. It may be only coincidental, but there is reason to believe that one follows the other. In any event, since the development of the modern city is so new in our total experience it is dangerous to assume that the human race can evolve rapidly enough to adjust to the ever-accelerating rate of change in our environment caused by urbanization.
I believe we are not fully aware of all the effects overcrowding and stress have on human beings, either from a psychological or physiological point of view. There is statistical evidence in growing amounts which would seem to indicate that the megalopolis is not the most desirable or beneficial environment for the human being.
For example, the impact of crime seems to be highest in urban centres. Drug abuse follows the same trend. We seem to have the highest rate of emotional instability and poor health in urban centres, especially where they contain slums and poor housing. We have the recent phenomenon of riots, protests and urban guerillas. Indeed, it could be argued that civilizations of the past collapsed after they became over-urbanized.
The second reason for my concern is that the rampant growth of a few large centres is not only creating horrendous problems for them in such fields as housing, pollution, crime, health, the cost of living and so on, but is at the same time sapping the vitality of the rural and small town segment of Canadian life.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Human Environmental Studies

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
The services needed by the population- government services, medical institutions, and educational institutions-are, I believe, being unnecessarily over-concentrated in our large urban centres. For example, I believe the federal government's services are over-concentrated in the capital region.
Urbanization on the scale presently taking place ignores the fact that man is part of the web of life. Very high concentrations of human beings give off pollutants, and in modern civilizations the amount of pollutants given off is larger per capita than it used to be. The amount of pollutants given off is so high and in such concentration that it cannot be assimilated or purified by the process of nature. The processes of nature are swamped in this regard. Water, soil and air pollution result, to say nothing of pollution by noise. Many of our unplanned, rapidly growing cities are, from an ecological point of view, festering sores on the face of mother earth.
I believe there is an optimum size for cities. I do not know what it is, but I have the notion that many of our larger Canadian cities have probably passed that size already. For a city to boast that it is the most rapidly growing community in the world is like someone saying he has the fastest growing cancer in town. It is not necessarily a good thing. We should be astute enough to realize that bigness is not synonymous with quality. The dinosaurs found that out, and they are now extinct.
Some of our cities are already collapsing under their own weight as far as financing and administration are concerned. The result is they have to be subsidized by provincial governments. Provincial governments in turn have to be subsidized by the federal government. The net result is that rural and small town Canada ends up subsidizing our largest urban centres.
I am a strong believer in the philosophy that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. We should not be proud of the large segment of our national wealth which we now deem it necessary to apply for cleaning up pollution and that sort of thing. It would have been much smarter to have taken preventive measures some years ago. That would have made this unnecessary.
If we do not take preventive measures now, the problems will become insoluble. The situation is extremely serious. The question is what to do about it. Can anything be done about it? We would be met immediately with the argument that it is not a federal responsibility. The cities and municipalities are a creation of the provinces. Of course there is a divided jurisdiction but I think this is an issue which has to be faced in the national interest before we can make any real progress toward the improvement of the urban environment.
In December, 1967, the prime minister of that day made the following suggestion:
Before we can make any real progress toward an improvement in our urban environment we must first improve the planning of the environment. The need for such improved planning has already been widely recognized. To help meet this need I would like to propose the establishment jointly by the federal and provincial governments of a council on housing and urban development whose functions, generally, would be to gather and publish comprehensive, objective and regular assess-


Human Environmental Studies
ments of housing and urban development needs across the country and to suggest priorities of need and plans to meet them.
The federal government is prepared to participate at once in the establishment and maintenance of such a continuing council.
That was an excellent suggestion but, as far as I know, it died right there and nothing ever came of it. I believe there is growing evidence that the direction in which we are moving is bad. Can we do anything about it? Can we reverse the trend? I think we can. After all thousands, perhaps millions of people, migrate to the large cities not by choice but because of economic pressures. That is where the jobs are. Of course the question is: why are the jobs there?
I believe the jobs are there because industries decide to settle in or near the large population centres from their own selfish point of view-the profit motive; considering only the balance sheet. They have no responsibility for facing the many problems which are generated by their decision to locate in an overcrowded area. They do not need to worry about where employees are going to live, who will build roads for them to travel on or schools for their children to attend.
I believe that if a tax, even if it were only symbolic, were levied on such enterprises commensurate with the social problems they create their decisions would be different, and we would find these industries locating in a more dispersed fashion to the benefit of all Canadians. We might then be able to contemplate sensible, even growth throughout the country, something which would put the problems of pollution control, housing, education, medical care and all the other requisites for a good life within our capacity to meet.

Mr. Speaker, it is a particular pleasure for me to rise to take part in this discussion because I am a new member of parliament, and I am pleased to have had the opportunity to participate both in the debate on Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and even this early in other business of the House.
I am interested in the proposition put before us by the hon. member opposite. I think he shares the concerns felt by many Canadians, and I want to say to him that the majority of the concerns he put forward are those which I, too, share. I think the only question which I would raise is whether we really do need another institute, commission, or other type of bureaucracy to do this. In my opinion I think the concerns brought forward are being addressed and researched by the Ministry of the Environment, a ministry being led by a most capable minister, and I think those concerns are being well expressed both in the government and to the country.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
I understand that the procedure followed during this hour is such that members can express personal points of view they may hold on the subjects brought before us. In that context, I would like to make two or three comments on the question of the environment, respecting its importance and some of the things which should be more or less obvious, although the environment

cannot be the only thing about which we are terribly concerned.
I have some background in environmental matters-in fact I have done some studies in that area. I have practised some of the concepts that environmentalists raised a number of years ago, perhaps even before this was a very popular thing in which everybody wanted to be involved. So, Mr. Speaker, I think I have an appreciation of the overall view of how important the environment is to us.
If we fail to take note of how important the environment is, and fail to do some of the things we must do at this point, then our entire future, indeed, the very nature and shape of this country, will be greatly affected.
Certainly the government recognizes that fact. If it had not done so it would not have set up Environment Canada and, most important of all, it would not have made the announcement it made very recently to the effect that all major projects pertaining to the government would be subject to an environmental assessment before they could proceed. I think this is a proper procedure, bearing in mind that some of the projects in which we will be involved over the next few years will have very great environmental impact on the country. It is only right and just that a body which has some depth of knowledge should look at these projects purely from an environmental point of view.
I would like to raise two concerns which this subject brings to my mind. One is in the area of energy. I said, when making my maiden speech, that by the year 2,000 we will be using two and one half times as much energy as we are at the present time. That is a rather incredible fact when one stops to think about it. Frankly, very recently concern has been expressed as to whether we have the adequacy within Canada to meet some of the energy needs which will arise in such a short time-a period of perhaps another 25 years.
One of the things which I think is not fully appreciated is that, in the past, the environmental concern relating to energy has been in almost direct opposition to those who care very much about conservation and efficient utilization of energy. I say this because much of the environmental concern has led industry, which is a very large user of energy, to change from coal and crude oil to natural gas. In fact a large amount of the electricity used in Canada is generated by natural gas.
I think this was a logical decision for industries to make when they were faced with meeting environmental regulations. After all, natural gas is a commodity which is reasonably priced and which does meet environmental concerns. But in a country which has a lot of lower grade energy it does seem to raise the question of whether it would not have been better in certain instances to have tackled the environmental program head-on through the use of increased technology.
Would we not have been better to have used such energy sources as coal and heavy crude oil more effectively and thus not be so concerned at this point in time about whether we have an adequate supply of natural gas? I would remind the House that perhaps much of the energy concern, or crisis as it is called in the United States, was brought about by this very situation, the very fact that


much of its industry, including a great part of its electrical utility system changed its input of energy from coal and heavy crude to high grade energy such as natural gas.
With the scarcity which has developed they now experience a problem which it is difficult for them to overcome. We are very fortunate in this country, of course, to have an abundant supply of uranium. It seems to me that using uranium, and using it through the CANDU process, answers very well the two concerns at the same time, that is, the concern of the environmentalists and the conservation of energy, which is equally important.
I want to raise another question and that is the relationship of the environment in the large urban centres to the environment in the very fragile part of the north of this very large country.
When the debate on the Mackenzie valley pipe line comes before the House and the country, I think it will centre mainly on the aspect of environmental assessment and the impact that it will have. I remind everyone that it is difficult, unless we are really prepared to pay the price, to have it both ways. As a person who lives in an urban centre I can understand that we want a much better environment within our large and growing urban areas. But we must realize that in achieving this, it will have an impact on the environment in the far north. We must also understand that if we are to preserve the environment in the far north and keep it intact, we must perhaps be prepared not to have such a high quality environment in the urban centres. Perhaps the proper decision will be made, that we should have concern for both. But all Canadians will have to pay in order to honour both those commitments.
Another area of concern is the conservation of first-class, prime agricultural land. I seem to sense that many of the projects being thought about and evaluated at this point in time, such as utility power lines, highways, pipe lines and urban growth, are subject to environmental assessment. If one thinks about this, and about all the other aspects of environmental assessment, it leads one to the conclusion that the best place to locate many of these facilities would perhaps be on our best agricultural land, where the impact is least on the environment.
I think that this is the wrong approach. Th^.best agricultural land that we have in this country is a very precious commodity, a commodity that should have at least equal consideration with environmental concern. After all, we have an expanding population to feed in Canada. I also think we have a moral responsibility to help feed the many millions of people in the world who need our agricultural products. The point that I want to make is that we must take a very balanced view in order to make sure that we look after both aspects.
I was interested to hear the hon. member opposite express concern for the environment within the large urban areas, which is a good point. I should like to see it extended to include concern for the health of Canadians. I was alarmed to read in the minister's recent publication that the cost of health care for Canadians has now reached something like 9.1 per cent of personal income, or over $300 for every man, woman and child in Canada. In the
Human Environmental Studies same publication the point is made that part of this is due to the environment in which we live.
Surprisingly, it is stated that nearly half of hospital bed time is given over to sicknesses due to stress, perhaps due to our life style in this highly urbanized society in which we live. Suicide is now the second most frequent cause of death among people aged 15 and 30. I guess I am repeating some of the arguments made by the hon. member opposite who related that over 90 per cent of all Canadians now live on less than 7 per cent of our land, while 80 per cent live in or close to large urban centres.
We must realize that we are living in times of stress, with much pressure on the family unit. In this regard we must make a serious assessment and determine its impact on the environment. We must fund and carry out studies that will tell us how big our urban centres should be allowed to grow, and how much the level of stress should be allowed to rise, so as not to reach the point where it becomes of concern to us all.
May I raise one other matter into which concern for the environment should be projected. It is a matter in which I am very interested, and about which not too much is known. I refer to labour-management negotiations. It would seem that on the surface the number of difficult settlements of labour-management disputes should be decreasing. After all, we have more affluence in this country perhaps than ever before. But really, Mr. Speaker, the opposite is true: we are having more difficult settlements, both in terms of finance and in terms of number.
It seems to me that most of this difficulty relates not so much to the financial aspect of a settlement as to the work environment, to the fact that we take an individual and put him in a situation where he is just plain bored, where he is dehumanized, and feels a total loss of identity. Such a worker feels he is not really participating in any area of creativity, whereas he was previously.
Our society is really to blame for that. We are fast becoming a society of big business, big government, big unions-just plain bigness. This is a very difficult thing for the individual to cope with, and I contend we should be doing some environmental studies within the industrial setting. We should study noise levels, colour, sense of accomplishment, creativity and that sort of thing which will affect productivity in this country, which will perhaps allow the individual to have a greater sense of accomplishment, and perhaps improve the physical and mental health of our workers.
Another matter which we should consider is uniformity of application of environmental regulations. It seems to me that we have a situation where Canadian companies are competing with each other, where some companies are faced with stringent environmental regulations and others are not. In fact, some companies are attracted to areas where there are lax environmental regulations, whereas other areas practise environmental concern very highly.
To this end, a few days ago I was pleased to note that the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) started to publish some national guidelines. These guidelines will be of great help, not only to the provinces and authorities that will administer them but to industry as well. If industry meets these guidelines then there will be some


Human Environmental Studies degree of uniformity of environmental standards all across Canada.
In spite of concern in this country for the environment,
I think we are very fortunate in Canada. We have a good degree of lead time compared with some other industrialized countries in the world. We can do something to preserve our environment so we will have a better future.
I hope that a good deal of the spending by the Minister of the Environment, and by industry itself, will be directed toward environmental research.
It seems to me there is a clear role for the federal government. It should show leadership in conducting research into the environment and into hardware to help preserve the environment. The carrying out of this role is the single most effective way of getting industry, on a voluntary basis, to upgrade its environmental standards. I do not think it is being fair to be hard on industry when industry has very little confidence in the type of equipment that is available to preserve the environment.
Before my time is up I should like to say that no one more than myself appreciates the concern for the environment expressed by the hon. member opposite. We need to work very diligently on improving our technology and giving leadership to industry. We should move away somewhat from the focus of the past, where we dealt essentially with air and water, and look more at the human side-job satisfaction, the health of Canadians, and improvement of our national productivity. We must concern ourselves about solid waste and other matters. We must seek a balanced solution to our environmental problems since there are other problems of equal importance.
I conclude by saying that the matter raised by the hon. member is of concern. That concern is shared by everyone in this House. I should just like to put the proposition to him that all these matters are being very adequately analysed by the Minister of the Environment at this time.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
This afternoon we are discussing a motion by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) to set up an institute of human environmental studies to explore and make recommendations in respect of various aspects of pollution of the environment. In reading over the motion I see that it is rather detailed, involving many areas, and contains considerable merit.
I think environmental pollution is a subject about which everyone has an opinion. Very much like motherhood, everyone is in favour of protecting the environment, but when it comes to proposing practical solutions and, more important, when we in the government are asked to do something about it, the history of protection of the environment in this country is indeed sad.
When we talk about the environment we must not forget the world situation. We must look at Canada in context with world environment. We see a pretty frightening situation on a world scale. The real problem in respect t o pollution and preserving the environment boils down to our basic concept of a belief in growth. If we analyse the individual attitude in Canada, and the Canadian government attitude, we must conclude that for sometime we have accepted the concept that growth per se is good, and

we have ended up with a situation in which it seems we are headed on a collision course as far as the environment is concerned.
Looking at the world scale, because we are not an island unto ourselves and will be affected by what is happening to the world environment, we find that the human population on this planet is growing by about 70 million people per year, demanding more food, water, fuel and so on. We have a responsibility in the world community, especially in these days when we see the spectre of starvation in Africa and South America, to help our fellow world citizens.
Yet when we look at our own country and our attitude toward consumption I am afraid we can be indicted as being some of the worst gluttons as far as resources are concerned. For example, if we were to extend the living standard in this country on a world scale, the demand on the resources of this planet would be astronomical. If we were to project Canada's standards worldwide, by the year 2000 the world would need about 1,300 per cent more aluminum, 900 per cent more copper, and 700 per cent more iron than we now consume. Yet when we look at world deposits of precious fuel minerals, coal for example, we find that we only have projections for three to four centuries, and for petroleum and natural gas projected reserves for only the next 70 or 80 years.
Some say we can turn to nuclear power, but here we encounter the problem of storing radio active material, and problems again of pollution. The people of Pickering are worried at the moment about the whole business of cooling the nuclear plant there, resulting in hot pollution in our water system.
In May, 1969, the United Nations pointed out that because of our lack of concern about the environment, already on this planet 1!4 billion acres of arable land have been lost to mankind through mismanagement. The reliance of modern technology on the combustion of fossil fuels has brought a 10 per cent increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide over the past century, and this could rise to 25 per cent by the end of this century. In North America alone automobiles account for 60 per cent of the air pollution of the continent. Yet how many of us are not so endeared to the automobile that we would try other forms of urban transportation in order to lessen this pollution, or pressure industry to go ahead full speed on anti-pollution devices for automobiles?
What I am saying is that we must be concerned with world environment rather than just looking inward, being concerned just with the environment in Canada. When we look at our environment we do not see a very encouraging record. It is all fine and good to set up an institute to carry out additional studies on the environmental situation, but if existing provincial and federal governments had applied the law that is already on the books with some vigour, we would be a long way down the road in cleaning up the environment.
The trouble has been not only a lack of will among provincial and federal governments to get serious about anti-pollution legislation, but there has also been a lack of coordination between the two levels of government. We have many overlapping and competing agencies, and because we have different provincial standards of pollu-


tion controls industry plays one province off against another, saying it will not locate in a certain province because its anti-pollution laws are too strict, but will move elsewhere. It is important that we have national pollution standards. This can only be attained by vigorous action on the part of the federal government, and I am sorry to say that this has been lacking to this day.
Canada has additional problems in respect to our international boundary. In my constituency, which borders on the Great Lakes, there has been real difficulty in getting co-operation between American states, the U.S. federal government, the province of Ontario and our federal government in order to clean up the Great Lakes. Already Lake Superior is endangered by the deposit of asbestos fibres or taconite tailings near Duluth, Minnesota. It seems to me we just cannot rely on the federal government to look for national standards in this country. There has to be active co-operation with the United States.
Why have we not been more serious in this country in grappling with the problem of pollution? In addition to a lack of coordination I am afraid that politicians and many Canadians have accepted the propaganda of many offending industries, that to adopt strong pollution, control would mean the closing down of plants with ultimate unemployment. This myth should be put to rest once and for all.
For example, in the Unites States the federal government carried out a very comprehensive survey to discover the effects of a strong pollution control system on the unemployment rate. The finding was that only .05 per cent of the total working force would be affected by tough anti-pollution measures against industry, and that this low rate of unemployment could certainly be offset by creative anti-pollution employment programs for those people who may be thrown out of work because of the closing of some very antiquated and badly run industrial plants.
For example, Mr. Speaker, there is a great need in this country to upgrade and build new sewage treatment facilities at the municipal level. We could employ thousands of Canadians in our labour force to do a very worthwhile and significant job of dealing with that one problem of pollution. I am afraid that all too often Liberal and Conservative governments have bowed to the pressures of some of the large corporations and business concerns in this country when it came to proposing tough anti pollution legislation.
I remember very vividly the Conservative government of Ontario, when it was first elected in 1971, saying that it was going to bring in tough laws against disposable bottles, but here we are in 1974 still awaiting some kind of significant legislation dealing with that problem.
In the few minutes that remain I should like to propose some solutions. I think it is important that what we say here today be considered seriously by the Minister of the Environment. First of all, to do something significant about pollution control we need national standards for environmental quality, and these standards must be set for air, water and land. But the point is that they should
Human Environmental Studies be set based on the biology of the environment and not on what is technologically possible.
Besides having standards we must become serious about the penalties that we impose for the violation of these standards. How laughable it is when a large corporation is fined $200 for violating some anti pollution law. It spends more than that on paper clips in a year. How Corporations must laugh at our seriousness in tackling the problem of pollution when our penalties are so minimal!
The second thing I would propose is that the cost of pollution control be met either directly by the offending party, or by a subsidy provided by the government. In the case of a subsidy, it should certainly be made public for our scrutiny. I think we should also have the government institute low cost loans to municipalities and some industries for sewage treatment plants and plant clean ups. This is vital. Also, as I mentioned earlier, non-recyclable throw away consumer products should be phased out by law.
I also think that the Department of the Environment should co-ordinate and enforce all environmental control legislation. The department should be given the task of scrutinizing all activities in the country for their potential environmental impact. But if we are serious about the problem of growth and how it contributes to the ruining of the environment and to pollution, we must embark on a program of conservation, especially of our non renewable resources.
Fossil fuels and scarce minerals should be conserved. Near my riding of Sault Ste. Marie is the riding of Sudbury, and there is situated the great International Nickel Mine. I have seen projections which show that with the high rate of exploiting the nickel at that mine right now the mine's life is only some 30 to 35 years. Many minerals should be recycled rather than just dumped. To this end we need research to develop a comprehensive policy of recycling.
Our energy demands must be reduced. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) is talking about conserving energy in this country. I would like to see a really forceful program, not just tokenism such as turning off the lights around Parliament Hill.
I think that resource developers must also assess the potential effects of their projects on the environment before undertaking them. We have learnt to our dismay what has happened to the Mackenzie River delta because of the Bennett dam in British Columbia. No surveys were carried out prior to that construction, and the federal government stands condemned in the eyes of the Canadian people for the whole process of the development of James Bay and the lack of prior environmental studies there. I fear that within the next couple of years the whole issue of the Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline will be rammed down our throats without proper environmental studies being done first.
We should also set aside ecological reserves in the wilderness to prevent the total disappearance of many of our species of animals in this country. We should also undertake research of all Arctic environmental problems, and also in regard to population and the problems of growth there. Canada could take a leading role to initiate, through the United Nations, an international conference to pro-
542


Human Environmental Studies mote the stabilization of the earth's population. We must conduct research into human settlement problems, particularly those of the urban areas, to prevent overcrowding and the megalopolises that have plagued so many people in the over-industrialized areas of the world.
I commend the hon. member for Malpeque for his attempt to bring to the attention of the government the seriousness of the problem of pollution in this country and the need to protect the environment. It seems to me that we must no longer be content to measure progress by industrial growth or the gross national product because short term gain often brings long term damage.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTITUTE OF HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the points mentioned by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), and enlarged upon in his speech this afternoon, are certainly of those which seriously concern Canadians.
Though public attention is concentrated mostly at this time on such extremely important matters as inflation, energy supplies, food products, on a national and international basis, it is imperative that factors related to the environment not be neglected in the overall steps to be taken in achieving our society of tomorrow. As I shall explain briefly, those factors are now the subject of serious and imaginative attention on the part of the government.
The extent of the problems referred to in the motion of the hon. member for Malpeque indicates the complexity of the points he made. Social, economic and scientific factors must be considered together if we are to determine what constitutes a satisfactory environment. There is no simple or magic formula to tell us exactly what a satisfactory environment is. Mr. Speaker, all one has to do is glance back at the last two decades to see what today's citizens want in the line of housing, transportation, education, health care and leisure, and to realize that we have come a long way beyond the public opinion of barely a few years ago. And what the public will be calling for tomorrow will still be very different.
There is also a new concern, that of seeing the economic development adjusted to the cost of environment. Those costs are more readily accepted as part of the normal costs of economic development. What will be the conditions in some twenty years?
Finally, it is important to know better what effects environmental pollution has on health. The matter is related to the scientific field and consequently it is not liable to change. However, once the basic facts are known, some social pressures could demand periodical changes in the control standards which are the result of such knowledge. In addition, as the scientific methodology is improving, new discoveries can lead to different conclusions about the consequences of environmental pollution on the human and ecologic systems.
Much work is under way in those various fields not only in Canada but also in other countries and performed as well by international organizations.
In Canada, a number of specific steps have been taken in this area. Mr. Speaker, I think it is useful to refer, as a starting point, to the government's decision establishing

the Department of Environment and the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, which is now under the very able leadership of the new Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). On the one hand, the former has been designed as an operating department with specific responsibilities in the extension and review of measures relating to air, water, soil, fisheries, forests and wildlife. On the other, the latter has been set up as a kind of policy architect in an area generally considered as provincial in jurisdiction.
A good number of other federal departments and agencies retained responsibilities over environment, but the Department of Environment has been given the mandate to coordinate all federal activities relating to environment. A positive effort has been made in this area to ensure a more effective coordination between the various departments and generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, this measure has been useful. This is mostly the result of a series of mechanisms and the good will of the people involved in the environment problem.
As to the particular questions mentioned in the motion introduced by the hon. member for Malpeque, among the activities most directly related to the federal government are those of the National Research Council Joint Committee which is investigating the scientific criteria regulating the quality of the environment. This committee is made up of experts from government, industries and universities. Its aim is to collect and evaluate scientific information throughout the world concerning the effects of pollutants on living organisms and human beings. Such assessments constitute a solid basis for institutions like the Department of the Environment when controls are required.
That department has also come up with a process permitting it to review and evaluate environmental protection. It has been conceived so as to make sure that federal activities in the environmental field be scrutinized as to their probable impact on environment before being given approval.
Mr. Speaker, the speech I had intended to deliver was much longer. It would have been of special interest to those who are not familiar with Boileau's language, because they could have heard the latter part of it in the language of Shakespeare.
